notes.text: Today — Even at this time, notwithstanding all your pretended consolations. Stroke - The hand or stroke of God upon me. Groaning - Doth exceed my complaints.
O — I desire nothing more than his acquaintance and presence; but alas, he hides his face from me. Seat - To his throne or judgment-seat to plead my cause before him.
Know — If he should discover to me any secret sins, for which he contendeth with me, I would humble myself before him, and accept of the punishment of mine iniquity.
No — He would not use his power against me, but for me; by enabling me to plead my cause, and giving sentence according to that clemency, which he uses towards his children.

There — At that throne of grace, where God lays aside his majesty, and Judges according to his wonted clemency. Dispute - Humbly propounding the grounds of their confidence. So - Upon such a fair and equal hearing. Delivered - From the damnatory sentence of God. This and some such expressions of Job cannot be excused from irreverence towards God, for which God afterwards reproves him, and Job abhorreth himself.
Is not — As a judge to hear and determine my causes, otherwise he knew God was essentially present in all places.

glossa.text: « And Job answering said: Now also in bitterness. » ((GREG.)) The mind of the just man is always in bitterness, etc., *as far as* who seek to seduce by sweet speeches.
« And the hand of my stroke. » Now the hand of the stroke is the strength of the smiting; but because out of adversities the just thirst the more for the face of their author, there follows:

« Who will grant me. » The elect, when they see anything whatever done against their wish, run back to the hidden judgments of God, that in them they may see that what seems to run without in disorder is not disposed within in disorder. And this is what he adds:

« That I might find him. » As it is: that God now defers, so that he may be the more desired.

« And come even to his throne. » The throne is the angels, etc., *as far as* while they see that God disposes better things, whence:

« I will set judgment before God. » To set judgment before God, etc., *as far as* to consider how terrible the judge, now hidden and silent, will afterwards appear.
« I will fill my mouth. » Because, while he contemplates the judge's examination against himself, he pursues himself bitterly with the invective of penance.

That I may know the words which, » etc. For when we pursue our faults by repenting, we find what the judge could say to us about them in his examination: which he does not know, because he neglects his own evils.

« I would not that he contend with much strength. » For who could be found just in the examination, if God should sift the life of men according to the majesty of his strength: for however just a man be, if he is strictly judged, he is pressed by the mass of that greatness, whence he adds:

« Nor of greatness. » As if he should say: If he contended with me according to his strength, he would press me with his own mass. And note that, while he shuns the strength, he desires the weakness of the incarnation, whence he adds:
« Let him set forth equity. » The mediator of God and of men, etc., *as far as* as victor I may bring forth the judgment of my absolution.
« If to the east. » ((Ibid.)) As if he should say: the incarnate Son, etc., *as far as* But not even in all these does the soul fully know itself, whence:

notes.text: My God — Who art my friend and father, though now thou frownest upon me. The repetition denotes, the depth of his distress, which made him cry so earnestly. Forsaken - Withdrawn the light of thy countenance, the supports and comforts of thy spirit, and filled me with the terrors of thy wrath: this was in part verified in David, but much more fully in Christ. Roaring - My out-cries forced from me, by my miseries.

But thou art — Just and true in all thy ways, this he adds to strengthen his faith, and to enforce his prayers, and prevail with God for the honour of his holy name, to hear and help him. Inhabitest - Whom thy people are perpetually praising.
A worm — Neglected and despised. People - Not only of the great men, but also of the common people. Which doth not so truly agree to David as to Christ.
Shoot out — They gape with their mouths, in mockery. This and the next verse are applied to Christ, Matt. xxvii, 39, 43.
Bulls — Wicked and violent, and potent enemies; for such are so called, Ezek xxxix, 18 Amos iv, 1. Of Bashan - As the cattle there bred were, and therefore fierce and furious.

Water — My spirits are spent and gone like water which once spilt can never be recovered; my very flesh is melted within me, and I am become as weak as water. Bones - I am as unable to help myself, and as full of torment, as if all my bones were disjointed. Wax - Melted, through fear and overwhelming grief.

Dried — I have in a manner no more moisture left in me, than is in a dry potsherd. Cleaveth - Through excessive thirst and drought. Death - Thy providence, delivering me into the power of mine enemies, and by thy terrors in my soul.

glossa.text: *God, my God.* ((CASS.)) A complaint of being forsaken is set before, and prayer also, as in all the psalms of the passion. ((AUG., CASS.)) *God, my God:* he doubles it out of affection, or *God* of all through the power of creation, *mine* properly through worship. ((AUG.)) When he had said this on the cross, he shewed that this psalm was written of himself. *Look upon me.* ((CASS.)) It is not in the Hebrew, but was added by the seventy interpreters. *Why hast thou forsaken me?* ((AUG.)) This is a wonder, since God also was with him; but it was for us, who in him are his body. *Far from my salvation,* that is, from that of my old man, because *salvation is far from sinners,* and these are the words not of justice, but of sins. Or, far from salvation are the words of my sins, which are to be taken away.

*I shall cry.* ((AUG.)) He speaks of us, of his own body, as when perchance he says: *Let this chalice pass from me,* that is, he is thought to have feared to die; but he said these things for his own weak ones who fear to die, and so this also is the voice of the members: *I shall cry and thou wilt not hear. By day, and thou wilt not hear, and by night, and not unto folly.* ((CASS.)) Because there are no shadows in him, and yet he is not heard unto bodily salvation.

*Thou dwellest in the holy place.* ((AUG.)) And so it is a wonder, because thou hast delivered the fathers; but I am a worm.

((CASS.)) Thou dwellest in the holy place, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. *The praise of Israel,* ((AUG.)) that is, of him that sees thee, not of him who wished to hide himself from thy sight.
*In thee have our fathers hoped: they have hoped.* ((CASS.)) It is a great beauty, while he repeats *they have hoped.*

*But I am,* etc. ((AUG.)) Thus far Christ in the person of the old man; here now he speaks properly in his own person. *But I am.* Now properly Christ: I was born without seed, that I might be beyond men in man, in whom I was made a reproach, that at least so the pride of man might imitate the humble. *A worm and no man, a reproach.* ((CASS.)) So vilely trodden down, etc., *as far as* a worm, born without coupling, mortal, humble and vile, creeping in silence.

*He hoped in the Lord,* etc. ((CASS.)) Saying: *Hope thou in the Lord,* etc. The irony of the Jews; behold, as it were a historical narration, not a prophecy, lest there be any excuse, lest there be any ambiguity.
*From the breasts.* Not from the time when I began to be suckled, etc., *as far as* but thou hast been my God. *From the womb.*

*From the womb.* ((AUG.)) Not only of a mother, which is the law of being born for all; but from the darkness of the Synagogue, in which he is unbelieving, not yet born into the light of Christ, who trusts in those carnal observances of the sabbath and of circumcision.

*Depart not from me,* thou who hast already begun.

*Thou hast drawn me out:* not a man; lest the virgin's childbearing be doubted, it was done by the power of God. *My hope from the breasts:* true humanity and great perfection; for from the breasts he does what one scarcely come of age can do.

*In thee was I cast,* not into the sins of man. Others are cast into Adam, whence they are guilty. *From my mother's womb, my God.* ((CASS.)) Neither was the conception without God, nor in sin, as man's is; whence the Angel: *The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee.*
*They have surrounded.* ((ID.)) The passion is described, which prayer concludes; to convince the Jews he relates things to come as though they were past.

*They have opened.* ((ID.)) As wild beasts wishing to swallow him down, their mouth, not unlocked unto wisdom. *As a lion.* ((AUG.)) As a lion seizing they surrounded him, as one roaring they opened their mouth.

*As water.* When water is poured out, etc., *as far as* whence, leaving him, they fled. ((CASS.)) As water is the sacrament of the washing away of sins, etc., *as far as* and it was made solid. *Like wax.* Well does he compare the mysteries of the law to wax, etc., *as far as* for they have surrounded. *In the midst of my belly.* ((AUG.)) The belly signifies the weak in the Church, or the memory of the Church.

*My strength is dried up like a potsherd.* ((CASS.)) Not as hay, but as a potsherd, which by fire is made the firmer. *My tongue.* ((AUG.)) They kept my precepts with them, through whom I was to speak: and through them I was brought down into the kindred of those who were the dust of death.

notes.text: For the word of God — Preached, ver. 2, and armed with threatenings, ver. 3. Is living and powerful - Attended with the power of the living God, and conveying either life or death to the hearers. Sharper than any two-edged sword - Penetrating the heart more than this does the body. Piercing - Quite through, and laying open. The soul and spirit, joints and marrow - The inmost recesses of the mind, which the apostle beautifully and strongly expresses by this heap of figurative words. And is a discerner - Not only of the thoughts, but also of the intentions.

In his sight — It is God whose word is thus "powerful:" it is God in whose sight every creature is manifest; and of this his word, working on the conscience, gives the fullest conviction. But all things are naked and opened - Plainly alluding to the sacrifices under the law which were first flayed, and then (as the Greek word literally means) cleft asunder through the neck and backbone; so that everything both without and within was exposed to open view.

Having therefore a great high priest — Great indeed, being the eternal Son of God, that is passed through the heavens - As the Jewish high priest passed through the veil into the holy of holies, carrying with him the blood of the sacrifices, on the yearly day of atonement; so our great high priest went once for all through the visible heavens, with the virtue of his own blood, into the immediate presence God.
He sympathizes with us even in our innocent infirmities, wants, weaknesses, miseries, dangers. Yet without sin — And, therefore, is indisputably able to preserve us from it in all our temptations.

Let us therefore come boldly — Without any doubt or fear. Unto the throne of God, our reconciled Father, even his throne of grace - Grace erected it, and reigns there, and dispenses all blessings in a way of mere, unmerited favour.

glossa.text:
*The word of God.* Which came from the royal seats. *Living.* Whom the unbelieving think dead. *Reaching.* Coming with entire consideration unto the separation of the soul, that is, of sensuality, and of the spirit, that is, of reason. *The division of the soul.* By the soul we live with the beasts, by the spirit we understand with the angels. And therefore by the soul are understood carnal sins, that is, those which are done by an act of the body, as lust. But by the spirit, spiritual ones, that is, those which are of the mind, as pride. But the word of God discerns between carnal sins and spiritual: who acts, what he acts, with what mind. *And of the spirit.* The word of God reaches with an inseparable knowledge, because it knows how sensuality is divided from reason, and itself from itself, when, being more given over to the lowest things, it is lower, or, called back from them, worthier. So too it sees how the spirit is divided from itself, whether while it gapes after God, thinking of the divine vision, or while lower down it considers heavenly things, or lower still on earth treats of worldly things to be rightly done, or how the spirit, that is, reason, is separated from sensuality, when that which is lower in itself surpasses that which is higher in her.

*Of the joints also.* A joint is called the joining of sensuality itself and of reason, which the Son of God sees; namely how they cohere with one another in something, or this and that, that is, reason and sensuality, how in their differences they agree with one another, when the higher difference of sensuality by consenting agrees with the differences of reason. Or the lower difference of reason, pressed down and captive, sometimes consents to the lower difference of sensuality. *Of the marrow.* Marrow, which is the inner part, is here said to be whatsoever is more inward and more subtle in the soul or in the spirit, which the Son of God also sees. For he discerns thoughts, that is, what diverse things diverse men think. He discerns also the intentions of those thoughts, whither each tends, to good or to evil. And, that I may say more, no creature earthly or heavenly is invisible to him, but all things are naked and uncovered, because on every side fully seen. Likewise he calls joints the conjunctions of thoughts: marrows, the intentions of them.

*Having therefore.* Here he begins to speak of Christ the high priest, how he is sufficient, and how he is worthier than the old priest. Whom also he changes, and the law which is under him, by his own better law, and how he is necessary to us for justice and salvation.

*For we have not,* etc. As if: Let us hold fast, and we ought to hold fast, because, since he is mighty, he is also merciful, having, as it were, experienced our infirmity. *Who cannot,* etc. It is impossible for a man who has not had experience of affliction, and has not sensibly borne all things, to know the afflictions of the afflicted. But Christ knows, not only in that he is God, according to which he knows all things, but in that he is man and has borne like things.

*In seasonable aid.* Now is the time of help, now is the time of gifts, when those who sin after baptism can through grace find repentance. But when the bride-chamber shall have been shut, when the king shall have come in to see those that recline, so that they who have been worthy of it shall have come to the bosom of the patriarch, then for the wicked it shall be the time of despair. But now, while the contest still remains and the palm hangs, there must be no despairing, but we must draw near with confidence, that is, without doubting, that by grace one may draw near, and seasonable aid be found. For there is a time which is not fitting.

notes.text: Matt. xix, 16; Luke xviii, 18.
He answering, said to him, Master — He stands reproved now, and drops the epithet good.

Jesus looking upon him — And looking into his heart, loved him - Doubtless for the dawnings of good which he saw in him: and said to him - Out of tender love, One thing thou lackest - The love of God, without which all religion is a dead carcass. In order to this, throw away what is to thee the grand hindrance of it. Give up thy great idol, riches. Go, sell whatsoever thou hast.

Jesus saith to them, Children — See how he softens the harsh truth, by the manner of delivering it! And yet without retracting or abating one tittle: How hard is it for them that trust in riches - Either for defense, or happiness, or deliverance from the thousand dangers that life is continually exposed to. That these cannot enter into God's glorious kingdom, is clear and undeniable: but it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a man to have riches, and not trust in them. Therefore, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter the kingdom.
Lo, we have left all — Though the young man would not.

He shall receive a hundred fold, houses, etc. — Not in the same kind: for it will generally be with persecutions: but in value: a hundred fold more happiness than any or all of these did or could afford. But let it be observed, none is entitled to this happiness, but he that will accept it with persecutions.

glossa.text: *A certain man running up, on bended knee. ((BEDA.))* He had heard, I believe, from the Lord that only those who wish to be like little ones are worthy of entrance into the heavenly kingdom, and therefore he desires to be more certain, not through parables but openly: by what merits of works he might be able to obtain eternal life.
*Why callest thou me good. ((ID.))* Because he had called him good master, etc., *as far as* but he testifies that apart from God there is no good.

*Thou shalt not commit adultery. ((ID.))* This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is set before us to be imitated, if we would enter the kingdom of God. And it is to be well noted that the justice of the law, kept in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods but also eternal life.
*Master. ((ID.))* He is not to be thought [to have asked] with the intent of one tempting, etc., *as far as* whence he adds: *Go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor ((Matth. V))*, etc.

*And come, follow me. ((ID.))* As if he said: After riches have been despised, imitate the Saviour, that is, evils being left behind, do good things. A money-bag is more easily despised than concupiscence or pleasure.
*How hardly. ((ID.))* They who apply themselves to the multiplying of riches, etc., *as far as* they may be able to enter the kingdom of God.

*It is easier for a camel.* How then in the Gospel did Matthew and Zacchaeus, and Joseph, and in the Old Testament very many rich men enter in? Perhaps because they held riches for nothing, or learned to despise them altogether, whence David: *I am alone and poor ((Psal. XXIV))*. And the same: *If riches abound, set not your heart upon them ((Ibid. LXI))*. He does not say, Do not receive them.
*And who can be saved.* Since there are more poor than rich, they would not have said this unless they had understood in the number of the rich all who would wish to obtain riches.
*With God.* Who is able to turn men from the greed of earthly things to the love of eternal things, and to make the proud humble.

*Behold, we have left all.* Great confidence: he was a fisherman, he was not rich, he sought his living by hand and craft, and yet he says confidently: *Behold, we have forsaken all things. And we have followed.* Because it is not enough so to leave, he joins that which is perfect, *and we have followed thee.* As if he said: We have done what thou didst command: what reward therefore wilt thou give?

*A hundredfold. ((BEDA.))* On this occasion certain men lay down as doctrine the Jewish fable of the thousand years after the resurrection of the just, etc., *as far as* they enjoy the most true love of the heavenly fatherland, which is signified by the right hand, and of all the elect alike.

*But many.* Because many begin but do not finish, a terrible sentence is subjoined: *But many,* etc. The thief on the cross, a confessor on the same day on which he was crucified for his own sins, by the grace of faith rejoices with Christ in paradise. Daily also we see many laymen excel rather by the merits of their life, and others, fervent from their earliest age in spiritual study, grow torpid at the last in idleness.

echoes.text: He has made my mouth like a sharp sword. He has hidden me in the shadow of his hand. He has made me a polished shaft. He has kept me close in his quiver.
echoes.note: ‘The word of God… sharper than any two-edged sword’ (v. 12) draws on the prophetic image of speech as a sword — the Servant's mouth ‘like a sharp sword’ in Isa 49:2. Verbal volume is the shared ‘sharp sword’ + ‘word/mouth’ collocation; Hays' criterion of thematic coherence (God's effective utterance) supports it, though Hebrews has no formula and the trope is widespread (cf. Isa 11:4; Eph 6:17; Rev 1:16).

echoes.text: Your all-powerful word leaped from heaven out of the royal throne, A stern warrior, into the midst of the doomed land, Bearing as a sharp sword your unfeigned commandment; And standing it filled all things with death; And while it touched the heaven it trode upon the earth.
echoes.note: The closest single parallel: in Wisdom God's hypostatized ‘all-powerful word’ (logos) is a warrior ‘bearing as a sharp sword’ God's commandment and is ‘living/active’ in execution. Hebrews shares the personification of the logos as a living, sword-bearing agent — a Second Temple commonplace the author and his hearers knew. Verbal volume (logos + sharp sword + active power) is high for an allusion; scholars (Beale & Carson) flag it as the proximate background.

echoes.text: You, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind; for Yahweh searches all hearts, and understands all the imaginations of the thoughts.
echoes.note: ‘Able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart’ (v. 12) restates the OT axiom that God ‘searches all hearts and understands every imagination of the thoughts.’ Thematic coherence is exact; the link is conceptual rather than verbatim, so allusion. The agent shifts from ‘Yahweh’ to ‘the word of God,’ which then resolves into ‘his sight… to whom we must give an account’ (v. 13).

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: A second witness to the heart-searching God who judges ‘according to his ways’ — coherent with Hebrews' ‘him to whom we must give an account’ (v. 13). Like 1 Chr 28:9 it supplies the conceptual substrate for the word that ‘discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart’; no verbal quotation, hence allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh looks from heaven. He sees all the sons of men. From the place of his habitation he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth, he who fashions all of their hearts; and he considers all of their works.
echoes.note: ‘There is no creature that is hidden from his sight’ (v. 13) echoes the psalmist's God who from heaven ‘sees all the sons of men… considers all their works.’ Low verbal volume; the coherence is the all-seeing, work-weighing gaze before which nothing is concealed.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: ‘Having then a great high priest… Jesus, the Son of God’ (v. 14) introduces, without citation, the high-priestly theme grounded in Ps 110:4 (quoted at 5:6; 7:17) — the verse that controls the whole central argument. No verbal volume here, but high recurrence in Hebrews makes the figural anticipation audible: the transition from the searching word to the sympathetic priest is the book's hinge.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.
echoes.note: The classic psalm of the inescapable, all-knowing gaze — God who knows the thought ‘from afar’ and every word ‘on my tongue.’ Faint and uncited, but thematically the nearest psalmic parallel to ‘no creature hidden from his sight… all things naked and laid open’ (vv. 12–13).

echoes.text: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
echoes.note: The striking word ‘naked’ (gymna) before God in v. 13 has a faint precursor in the wisdom topos that even Sheol lies ‘naked’ and ‘uncovered’ before God. Verbal volume rests on the single image of nakedness/exposure; widely noted as a faint echo (NA28/UBS margin).

echoes.text: Sheol and Abaddon are before Yahweh—how much more then the hearts of the children of men!
echoes.note: Parallel to Job 26:6, and closer still to Hebrews' move from cosmic exposure to the human heart: if Sheol lies open, ‘how much more the hearts of men.’ A faint a-fortiori echo behind ‘naked and laid open… the thoughts and intentions of the heart.’

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: The priest ‘who has passed through the heavens’ and the invitation to ‘draw near… to the throne of grace’ (vv. 14, 16) presuppose the enthronement of Ps 110:1, the catena's bracket (1:13; 10:12). Faint and figural — the throne-of-grace language assumes the session at the right hand the letter has already established.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: Jesus recites the second-table Decalogue commandments against murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and to honor father and mother, citing them as 'the commandments' the man knows. The wording follows the Decalogue directly. Highest Volume and explicit appeal to the Ten Words.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic recension of the same commandments is an equally valid source for Jesus' list, and the placement of 'Honor your father and mother' after the social prohibitions mirrors a known ordering. Marked as a parallel high-confidence citation alongside Exodus 20. The two Decalogue forms together secure the quotation.

echoes.text: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates.
echoes.note: Jesus' extra commandment 'Do not defraud' (not in the Decalogue) echoes the Deuteronomic prohibition against defrauding or oppressing a hired laborer and withholding wages. Mark's insertion of defrauding into a Decalogue list points to this legal tradition on economic injustice. The targeted addition to a rich landholder gives the allusion coherence.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
echoes.note: The Holiness Code's 'you shall not defraud your neighbor nor rob him; the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you overnight' is the strongest single source for Mark's 'Do not defraud.' Its pairing of fraud with withheld wages fits Jesus' demand that this wealthy man divest. Verbal contact on 'defraud' lifts this above generic.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: Jesus' rejoinder 'No one is good except one—God' reflects the Shema's confession of God's oneness and uniqueness, here applied to the predicate of goodness. The 'one' (heis) language coheres with Deuteronomic monotheism. The link is conceptual but anchored in the distinctive 'one God' formula.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'He who is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him' underwrites Jesus' logic that giving to the poor yields 'treasure in heaven.' The proverb's transaction of almsgiving credited with God grounds the heavenly-treasure promise. Coherence with the divestment command is strong.

echoes.text: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold.
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold' is the closest Second-Temple parallel to 'you will have treasure in heaven.' The instruction to convert wealth into a heavenly account, set beside almsgiving, matches Jesus' counsel precisely. Availability and verbal proximity make this a primary deuterocanonical source.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit instructs giving alms from one's possessions, promising that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure' and delivers from death. The almsgiving-as-stored-treasure theology directly parallels Jesus' 'give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.' The shared treasure-and-deliverance logic strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
echoes.note: 'Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good' is the recurrent liturgical confession that God alone is good, the conviction behind Jesus' 'No one is good except one—God.' The refrain pervades the Psalter (106, 107, 136). Low and contested: a diffuse liturgical commonplace rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase: so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.
echoes.note: Honoring the LORD with one's wealth and firstfruits, with promised reward, lies in the background of redirecting possessions toward God. The wisdom pattern of wealth surrendered and divinely repaid coheres with the pericope. Low and contested: thematic.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: The open-handed command to give freely to the poor brother and not harden the heart frames Israel's duty to the needy, which Jesus presses to its limit. The almsgiving ethic supplies background for 'give to the poor.' Contested; a broad covenantal commonplace.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?' is the canonical formula of divine possibility that Jesus restates as 'with men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.' Sarah's promised son against natural impossibility is the paradigm. The verbal and theological match (nothing too hard / all things possible) is strong.

echoes.text: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.
echoes.note: 'He who trusts in his riches will fall' directly underlies Jesus' qualification 'how hard is it for those who trust in riches to enter the Kingdom.' The verbal target is the verb of trusting in wealth, not merely possessing it. The proverb supplies both diagnosis and outcome, giving solid Volume.

echoes.text: Those who trust in their wealth, and boast in the multitude of their riches— none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.
echoes.note: Those who 'trust in their wealth' cannot by any means ransom a person from death, exactly the impossibility Jesus presses: riches cannot purchase entry or salvation. The psalm's link between trust-in-riches and the limits of ransom coheres with the chapter's later ransom saying. Conceptual overlap is precise and recurrent.

echoes.text: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.
echoes.note: 'I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted' is a near-formulaic source for 'all things are possible with God.' Job's confession of God's unbounded power matches Jesus' answer to 'who then can be saved?' The omnipotence formula recurs and coheres.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: Hannah's song declares the LORD makes poor and makes rich, raises the poor from the dust, and reverses high and low, undergirding 'many who are first will be last; and the last first.' The eschatological reversal of status and wealth coheres tightly with Jesus' promise and warning. The reversal motif is verbally and thematically apt.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant... should it also be marvelous in my eyes?' contrasts human limits with divine possibility in restoration. The reversal of what seems impossible to people coheres with Jesus' saying. Contested and low: thematic possibility-formula, no verbal lock.

echoes.text: Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,
echoes.note: 'Nothing is too hard for you' (Jeremiah's prayer) repeats the Genesis 18:14 omnipotence formula and reinforces Recurrence behind 'all things are possible with God.' Marked contested because Genesis 18:14 is the likelier primary source. Included for completeness of the divine-possibility tradition.

echoes.text: so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.
echoes.note: God 'sets on high those who are lowly,' the wisdom statement of divine reversal that informs the first-last saying. It supports the reversal pattern's Recurrence. Contested and low: general reversal topos.

echoes.text: Yahweh will grant you abundant prosperity, in the fruit of your body, in the fruit of your livestock, and in the fruit of your ground, in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers to give you.
echoes.note: Covenant blessing promises abundance of children, livestock, and land 'a hundredfold' in plenty, faintly behind the promise of houses, family, and lands 'one hundred times more.' The hundredfold-in-the-land blessing supplies background imagery. Contested; thematic and inexact.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac sows and reaps 'a hundredfold' because the LORD blessed him, a concrete OT instance of the hundredfold blessing language Jesus uses. It supplies Availability for 'one hundred times more.' Contested and low: a single lexical resonance.

notes.text: The house of Joseph — The kingdom of the ten tribes, the chief whereof was Ephraim, the son of Joseph. In Beth-el - If once this fire breaks out, all your idols in Beth-el shall not be able to quench it.

Ye — Rulers and Judges. Judgment - The righteous sentence of the law. To wormwood - Proverbially understood; bitterness, injustice and oppression. Leave off - Make to cease in your courts of judicature.
Teach us — To consider the shortness of life, and the certainty and speediness of death. That - That we may heartily devote ourselves to true wisdom.
Return — To us in mercy. How long - Will it be before thou return to us? Repent thee - Of thy severe proceedings against us.
Early — Speedily.

The beauty — His gracious influence, and glorious presence. In us - Do not only work for us, but in us, This psalm is a dialogue, wherein one declares the safety of them, who take God for their keeper, ver. 1. David declares this to be his resolution, ver. 2. Various promises are made to him, ver. 3-13. Which God himself confirms, ver. 14-16.

glossa.text:
*So make known thy right hand.* ((CASS.)) Thirdly, he prays and affirms deliverance. ((AUG.)) *Thy right hand.* He so *made known* Christ, etc., *as far as* that he may set him at the right hand.

*And them that are learned in heart in wisdom. Or, fettered in heart.* Which is the same thing, because they who are taught in wisdom thrust the foot of the mind into the fetters of God, that they may not stray from his way. These God so made known in the New Testament, that for faith they should spurn all things which are held great, in the Old, and should seek in eternal death: attending to this he speaks, on behalf of those who suffer many things from the world for the sake of eternal things.
*Turn thee.* As though his face were turned away from those in tribulation. *How long.* Elsewhere, a little. ((CASS.)) Not wholly, which profits the more, if some tribulation always admonishes us.

*In the morning we have rejoiced in thy mercy, and we have been delighted.* *delectatio* ((AUG., CASS.)) Now it is night, in which we hunger: but then we shall be filled with the countenance, whence: *I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear.* And elsewhere: *In the morning I will stand before thee, and will see.* But now instead of it *we have been glad,* even in the evil days in which we say: *Look upon thy servants.*

*Look upon thy servants.* What God does in himself, the Prophet prays may be done for his people: he prays, namely, that he may spare the sinning Jews, if not for their merits, at least for the sake of the works which he has wrought in them.

*And direct their children.* As if to say, even if they themselves have been scattered through iniquities *iniqui-tales*, at least the children, at the last, may be corrected by faith, who of themselves are depraved and unconvertible.

*The brightness of the Lord our God upon us, and work ye.* ((HIER., CASS.)) Let the image of God, restoring, be imprinted on the mind. Or the brightness of God is upon us, while we are adorned by the impress of the cross, and bear the standard of triumph on the forehead. ((CASS.)) For the image is threefold, etc., *as far as* that I may remember thee, understand thee, love thee.

notes.text: For the word of God — Preached, ver. 2, and armed with threatenings, ver. 3. Is living and powerful - Attended with the power of the living God, and conveying either life or death to the hearers. Sharper than any two-edged sword - Penetrating the heart more than this does the body. Piercing - Quite through, and laying open. The soul and spirit, joints and marrow - The inmost recesses of the mind, which the apostle beautifully and strongly expresses by this heap of figurative words. And is a discerner - Not only of the thoughts, but also of the intentions.

In his sight — It is God whose word is thus "powerful:" it is God in whose sight every creature is manifest; and of this his word, working on the conscience, gives the fullest conviction. But all things are naked and opened - Plainly alluding to the sacrifices under the law which were first flayed, and then (as the Greek word literally means) cleft asunder through the neck and backbone; so that everything both without and within was exposed to open view.

Having therefore a great high priest — Great indeed, being the eternal Son of God, that is passed through the heavens - As the Jewish high priest passed through the veil into the holy of holies, carrying with him the blood of the sacrifices, on the yearly day of atonement; so our great high priest went once for all through the visible heavens, with the virtue of his own blood, into the immediate presence God.
He sympathizes with us even in our innocent infirmities, wants, weaknesses, miseries, dangers. Yet without sin — And, therefore, is indisputably able to preserve us from it in all our temptations.

Let us therefore come boldly — Without any doubt or fear. Unto the throne of God, our reconciled Father, even his throne of grace - Grace erected it, and reigns there, and dispenses all blessings in a way of mere, unmerited favour.

glossa.text:
*The word of God.* Which came from the royal seats. *Living.* Whom the unbelieving think dead. *Reaching.* Coming with entire consideration unto the separation of the soul, that is, of sensuality, and of the spirit, that is, of reason. *The division of the soul.* By the soul we live with the beasts, by the spirit we understand with the angels. And therefore by the soul are understood carnal sins, that is, those which are done by an act of the body, as lust. But by the spirit, spiritual ones, that is, those which are of the mind, as pride. But the word of God discerns between carnal sins and spiritual: who acts, what he acts, with what mind. *And of the spirit.* The word of God reaches with an inseparable knowledge, because it knows how sensuality is divided from reason, and itself from itself, when, being more given over to the lowest things, it is lower, or, called back from them, worthier. So too it sees how the spirit is divided from itself, whether while it gapes after God, thinking of the divine vision, or while lower down it considers heavenly things, or lower still on earth treats of worldly things to be rightly done, or how the spirit, that is, reason, is separated from sensuality, when that which is lower in itself surpasses that which is higher in her.

*Of the joints also.* A joint is called the joining of sensuality itself and of reason, which the Son of God sees; namely how they cohere with one another in something, or this and that, that is, reason and sensuality, how in their differences they agree with one another, when the higher difference of sensuality by consenting agrees with the differences of reason. Or the lower difference of reason, pressed down and captive, sometimes consents to the lower difference of sensuality. *Of the marrow.* Marrow, which is the inner part, is here said to be whatsoever is more inward and more subtle in the soul or in the spirit, which the Son of God also sees. For he discerns thoughts, that is, what diverse things diverse men think. He discerns also the intentions of those thoughts, whither each tends, to good or to evil. And, that I may say more, no creature earthly or heavenly is invisible to him, but all things are naked and uncovered, because on every side fully seen. Likewise he calls joints the conjunctions of thoughts: marrows, the intentions of them.

*Having therefore.* Here he begins to speak of Christ the high priest, how he is sufficient, and how he is worthier than the old priest. Whom also he changes, and the law which is under him, by his own better law, and how he is necessary to us for justice and salvation.

*For we have not,* etc. As if: Let us hold fast, and we ought to hold fast, because, since he is mighty, he is also merciful, having, as it were, experienced our infirmity. *Who cannot,* etc. It is impossible for a man who has not had experience of affliction, and has not sensibly borne all things, to know the afflictions of the afflicted. But Christ knows, not only in that he is God, according to which he knows all things, but in that he is man and has borne like things.

*In seasonable aid.* Now is the time of help, now is the time of gifts, when those who sin after baptism can through grace find repentance. But when the bride-chamber shall have been shut, when the king shall have come in to see those that recline, so that they who have been worthy of it shall have come to the bosom of the patriarch, then for the wicked it shall be the time of despair. But now, while the contest still remains and the palm hangs, there must be no despairing, but we must draw near with confidence, that is, without doubting, that by grace one may draw near, and seasonable aid be found. For there is a time which is not fitting.

notes.text: Matt. xix, 16; Luke xviii, 18.
He answering, said to him, Master — He stands reproved now, and drops the epithet good.

Jesus looking upon him — And looking into his heart, loved him - Doubtless for the dawnings of good which he saw in him: and said to him - Out of tender love, One thing thou lackest - The love of God, without which all religion is a dead carcass. In order to this, throw away what is to thee the grand hindrance of it. Give up thy great idol, riches. Go, sell whatsoever thou hast.

Jesus saith to them, Children — See how he softens the harsh truth, by the manner of delivering it! And yet without retracting or abating one tittle: How hard is it for them that trust in riches - Either for defense, or happiness, or deliverance from the thousand dangers that life is continually exposed to. That these cannot enter into God's glorious kingdom, is clear and undeniable: but it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a man to have riches, and not trust in them. Therefore, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter the kingdom.
Lo, we have left all — Though the young man would not.

He shall receive a hundred fold, houses, etc. — Not in the same kind: for it will generally be with persecutions: but in value: a hundred fold more happiness than any or all of these did or could afford. But let it be observed, none is entitled to this happiness, but he that will accept it with persecutions.

glossa.text: *A certain man running up, on bended knee. ((BEDA.))* He had heard, I believe, from the Lord that only those who wish to be like little ones are worthy of entrance into the heavenly kingdom, and therefore he desires to be more certain, not through parables but openly: by what merits of works he might be able to obtain eternal life.
*Why callest thou me good. ((ID.))* Because he had called him good master, etc., *as far as* but he testifies that apart from God there is no good.

*Thou shalt not commit adultery. ((ID.))* This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is set before us to be imitated, if we would enter the kingdom of God. And it is to be well noted that the justice of the law, kept in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods but also eternal life.
*Master. ((ID.))* He is not to be thought [to have asked] with the intent of one tempting, etc., *as far as* whence he adds: *Go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor ((Matth. V))*, etc.

*And come, follow me. ((ID.))* As if he said: After riches have been despised, imitate the Saviour, that is, evils being left behind, do good things. A money-bag is more easily despised than concupiscence or pleasure.
*How hardly. ((ID.))* They who apply themselves to the multiplying of riches, etc., *as far as* they may be able to enter the kingdom of God.

*It is easier for a camel.* How then in the Gospel did Matthew and Zacchaeus, and Joseph, and in the Old Testament very many rich men enter in? Perhaps because they held riches for nothing, or learned to despise them altogether, whence David: *I am alone and poor ((Psal. XXIV))*. And the same: *If riches abound, set not your heart upon them ((Ibid. LXI))*. He does not say, Do not receive them.
*And who can be saved.* Since there are more poor than rich, they would not have said this unless they had understood in the number of the rich all who would wish to obtain riches.
*With God.* Who is able to turn men from the greed of earthly things to the love of eternal things, and to make the proud humble.

*Behold, we have left all.* Great confidence: he was a fisherman, he was not rich, he sought his living by hand and craft, and yet he says confidently: *Behold, we have forsaken all things. And we have followed.* Because it is not enough so to leave, he joins that which is perfect, *and we have followed thee.* As if he said: We have done what thou didst command: what reward therefore wilt thou give?

*A hundredfold. ((BEDA.))* On this occasion certain men lay down as doctrine the Jewish fable of the thousand years after the resurrection of the just, etc., *as far as* they enjoy the most true love of the heavenly fatherland, which is signified by the right hand, and of all the elect alike.

*But many.* Because many begin but do not finish, a terrible sentence is subjoined: *But many,* etc. The thief on the cross, a confessor on the same day on which he was crucified for his own sins, by the grace of faith rejoices with Christ in paradise. Daily also we see many laymen excel rather by the merits of their life, and others, fervent from their earliest age in spiritual study, grow torpid at the last in idleness.

echoes.text: He has made my mouth like a sharp sword. He has hidden me in the shadow of his hand. He has made me a polished shaft. He has kept me close in his quiver.
echoes.note: ‘The word of God… sharper than any two-edged sword’ (v. 12) draws on the prophetic image of speech as a sword — the Servant's mouth ‘like a sharp sword’ in Isa 49:2. Verbal volume is the shared ‘sharp sword’ + ‘word/mouth’ collocation; Hays' criterion of thematic coherence (God's effective utterance) supports it, though Hebrews has no formula and the trope is widespread (cf. Isa 11:4; Eph 6:17; Rev 1:16).

echoes.text: Your all-powerful word leaped from heaven out of the royal throne, A stern warrior, into the midst of the doomed land, Bearing as a sharp sword your unfeigned commandment; And standing it filled all things with death; And while it touched the heaven it trode upon the earth.
echoes.note: The closest single parallel: in Wisdom God's hypostatized ‘all-powerful word’ (logos) is a warrior ‘bearing as a sharp sword’ God's commandment and is ‘living/active’ in execution. Hebrews shares the personification of the logos as a living, sword-bearing agent — a Second Temple commonplace the author and his hearers knew. Verbal volume (logos + sharp sword + active power) is high for an allusion; scholars (Beale & Carson) flag it as the proximate background.

echoes.text: You, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind; for Yahweh searches all hearts, and understands all the imaginations of the thoughts.
echoes.note: ‘Able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart’ (v. 12) restates the OT axiom that God ‘searches all hearts and understands every imagination of the thoughts.’ Thematic coherence is exact; the link is conceptual rather than verbatim, so allusion. The agent shifts from ‘Yahweh’ to ‘the word of God,’ which then resolves into ‘his sight… to whom we must give an account’ (v. 13).

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: A second witness to the heart-searching God who judges ‘according to his ways’ — coherent with Hebrews' ‘him to whom we must give an account’ (v. 13). Like 1 Chr 28:9 it supplies the conceptual substrate for the word that ‘discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart’; no verbal quotation, hence allusion.

echoes.text: Yahweh looks from heaven. He sees all the sons of men. From the place of his habitation he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth, he who fashions all of their hearts; and he considers all of their works.
echoes.note: ‘There is no creature that is hidden from his sight’ (v. 13) echoes the psalmist's God who from heaven ‘sees all the sons of men… considers all their works.’ Low verbal volume; the coherence is the all-seeing, work-weighing gaze before which nothing is concealed.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: ‘Having then a great high priest… Jesus, the Son of God’ (v. 14) introduces, without citation, the high-priestly theme grounded in Ps 110:4 (quoted at 5:6; 7:17) — the verse that controls the whole central argument. No verbal volume here, but high recurrence in Hebrews makes the figural anticipation audible: the transition from the searching word to the sympathetic priest is the book's hinge.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.
echoes.note: The classic psalm of the inescapable, all-knowing gaze — God who knows the thought ‘from afar’ and every word ‘on my tongue.’ Faint and uncited, but thematically the nearest psalmic parallel to ‘no creature hidden from his sight… all things naked and laid open’ (vv. 12–13).

echoes.text: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
echoes.note: The striking word ‘naked’ (gymna) before God in v. 13 has a faint precursor in the wisdom topos that even Sheol lies ‘naked’ and ‘uncovered’ before God. Verbal volume rests on the single image of nakedness/exposure; widely noted as a faint echo (NA28/UBS margin).

echoes.text: Sheol and Abaddon are before Yahweh—how much more then the hearts of the children of men!
echoes.note: Parallel to Job 26:6, and closer still to Hebrews' move from cosmic exposure to the human heart: if Sheol lies open, ‘how much more the hearts of men.’ A faint a-fortiori echo behind ‘naked and laid open… the thoughts and intentions of the heart.’

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.’
echoes.note: The priest ‘who has passed through the heavens’ and the invitation to ‘draw near… to the throne of grace’ (vv. 14, 16) presuppose the enthronement of Ps 110:1, the catena's bracket (1:13; 10:12). Faint and figural — the throne-of-grace language assumes the session at the right hand the letter has already established.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: Jesus recites the second-table Decalogue commandments against murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and to honor father and mother, citing them as 'the commandments' the man knows. The wording follows the Decalogue directly. Highest Volume and explicit appeal to the Ten Words.

echoes.text: “Honor your father and your mother, as Yahweh your God commanded you; that your days may be long, and that it may go well with you, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you. “You shall not murder. “You shall not commit adultery. “You shall not steal. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor.
echoes.note: The Deuteronomic recension of the same commandments is an equally valid source for Jesus' list, and the placement of 'Honor your father and mother' after the social prohibitions mirrors a known ordering. Marked as a parallel high-confidence citation alongside Exodus 20. The two Decalogue forms together secure the quotation.

echoes.text: You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates.
echoes.note: Jesus' extra commandment 'Do not defraud' (not in the Decalogue) echoes the Deuteronomic prohibition against defrauding or oppressing a hired laborer and withholding wages. Mark's insertion of defrauding into a Decalogue list points to this legal tradition on economic injustice. The targeted addition to a rich landholder gives the allusion coherence.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbor, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
echoes.note: The Holiness Code's 'you shall not defraud your neighbor nor rob him; the wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you overnight' is the strongest single source for Mark's 'Do not defraud.' Its pairing of fraud with withheld wages fits Jesus' demand that this wealthy man divest. Verbal contact on 'defraud' lifts this above generic.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: Jesus' rejoinder 'No one is good except one—God' reflects the Shema's confession of God's oneness and uniqueness, here applied to the predicate of goodness. The 'one' (heis) language coheres with Deuteronomic monotheism. The link is conceptual but anchored in the distinctive 'one God' formula.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'He who is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him' underwrites Jesus' logic that giving to the poor yields 'treasure in heaven.' The proverb's transaction of almsgiving credited with God grounds the heavenly-treasure promise. Coherence with the divestment command is strong.

echoes.text: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold.
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will profit you more than gold' is the closest Second-Temple parallel to 'you will have treasure in heaven.' The instruction to convert wealth into a heavenly account, set beside almsgiving, matches Jesus' counsel precisely. Availability and verbal proximity make this a primary deuterocanonical source.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit instructs giving alms from one's possessions, promising that almsgiving 'lays up a good treasure' and delivers from death. The almsgiving-as-stored-treasure theology directly parallels Jesus' 'give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.' The shared treasure-and-deliverance logic strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.
echoes.note: 'Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good' is the recurrent liturgical confession that God alone is good, the conviction behind Jesus' 'No one is good except one—God.' The refrain pervades the Psalter (106, 107, 136). Low and contested: a diffuse liturgical commonplace rather than a citation.

echoes.text: Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase: so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.
echoes.note: Honoring the LORD with one's wealth and firstfruits, with promised reward, lies in the background of redirecting possessions toward God. The wisdom pattern of wealth surrendered and divinely repaid coheres with the pericope. Low and contested: thematic.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: The open-handed command to give freely to the poor brother and not harden the heart frames Israel's duty to the needy, which Jesus presses to its limit. The almsgiving ethic supplies background for 'give to the poor.' Contested; a broad covenantal commonplace.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?' is the canonical formula of divine possibility that Jesus restates as 'with men it is impossible, but not with God, for all things are possible with God.' Sarah's promised son against natural impossibility is the paradigm. The verbal and theological match (nothing too hard / all things possible) is strong.

echoes.text: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.
echoes.note: 'He who trusts in his riches will fall' directly underlies Jesus' qualification 'how hard is it for those who trust in riches to enter the Kingdom.' The verbal target is the verb of trusting in wealth, not merely possessing it. The proverb supplies both diagnosis and outcome, giving solid Volume.

echoes.text: Those who trust in their wealth, and boast in the multitude of their riches— none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.
echoes.note: Those who 'trust in their wealth' cannot by any means ransom a person from death, exactly the impossibility Jesus presses: riches cannot purchase entry or salvation. The psalm's link between trust-in-riches and the limits of ransom coheres with the chapter's later ransom saying. Conceptual overlap is precise and recurrent.

echoes.text: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.
echoes.note: 'I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted' is a near-formulaic source for 'all things are possible with God.' Job's confession of God's unbounded power matches Jesus' answer to 'who then can be saved?' The omnipotence formula recurs and coheres.

echoes.text: Yahweh makes poor, and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up. He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill, To make them sit with princes, and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s. He has set the world on them.
echoes.note: Hannah's song declares the LORD makes poor and makes rich, raises the poor from the dust, and reverses high and low, undergirding 'many who are first will be last; and the last first.' The eschatological reversal of status and wealth coheres tightly with Jesus' promise and warning. The reversal motif is verbally and thematically apt.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be marvelous in my eyes?” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: 'If it is marvelous in the eyes of the remnant... should it also be marvelous in my eyes?' contrasts human limits with divine possibility in restoration. The reversal of what seems impossible to people coheres with Jesus' saying. Contested and low: thematic possibility-formula, no verbal lock.

echoes.text: Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; there is nothing too hard for you,
echoes.note: 'Nothing is too hard for you' (Jeremiah's prayer) repeats the Genesis 18:14 omnipotence formula and reinforces Recurrence behind 'all things are possible with God.' Marked contested because Genesis 18:14 is the likelier primary source. Included for completeness of the divine-possibility tradition.

echoes.text: so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.
echoes.note: God 'sets on high those who are lowly,' the wisdom statement of divine reversal that informs the first-last saying. It supports the reversal pattern's Recurrence. Contested and low: general reversal topos.

echoes.text: Yahweh will grant you abundant prosperity, in the fruit of your body, in the fruit of your livestock, and in the fruit of your ground, in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers to give you.
echoes.note: Covenant blessing promises abundance of children, livestock, and land 'a hundredfold' in plenty, faintly behind the promise of houses, family, and lands 'one hundred times more.' The hundredfold-in-the-land blessing supplies background imagery. Contested; thematic and inexact.

echoes.text: Isaac sowed in that land, and reaped in the same year one hundred times what he planted. Yahweh blessed him.
echoes.note: Isaac sows and reaps 'a hundredfold' because the LORD blessed him, a concrete OT instance of the hundredfold blessing language Jesus uses. It supplies Availability for 'one hundred times more.' Contested and low: a single lexical resonance.

registers.label: Spare
lines: A man ran up and knelt: Good Teacher, what must I do?
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Go, sell what you have; then come, follow.
But his hands were full, and he went away grieving.
Who then can be saved?
For mortals it is impossible, but not for God.
Come, let us worship with open hands.
With God, all things are possible. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A man came running and fell on his knees: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? And Jesus, looking at him, loved him.
With God, all things are possible.
One thing you lack, he said: go, sell what you have, give it away, and you will have treasure in heaven. And the man's face fell, for he had much.
With God, all things are possible.
How hard it is to loosen our grip, to let our hands fall open, to seek good and not evil and live.
With God, all things are possible.
So come to the throne of grace and find mercy. Lay your burden down and worship.
With God, all things are possible. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: A rich man knelt and asked the way to life.
All things are possible with God.
Sell what you have, and come, follow me.
All things are possible with God.
Who then can be saved? For God, nothing is impossible.
All things are possible with God.
Come to the throne of grace and worship.
All things are possible with God. Amen.
